results.evidence: No statute numbers appear anywhere in the post; all legal rules described using general language like 'the legal limit,' 'depending on the model and jurisdiction,' and 'in most jurisdictions.'
No individual attorney or legal-scholar names appear; references are to organizations (Innocence Project, NHTSA) and publications (Forensic Science International, Journal of Analytical Toxicology).

All statistics are sourced: ±0.005–0.02 BAC margin (Forensic Science International), 375+ exonerations (Innocence Project), 1100:1–3500:1 partition ratio range (Journal of Analytical Toxicology), 2100:1 standard ratio qualified with 'in most jurisdictions.'

All procedural claims are jurisdiction-qualified: observation period '15 to 20 minutes (varies by jurisdiction),' calibration cycles 'every 30, 60, or 90 days depending on the model and jurisdiction,' partition ratio challenges 'viable in your jurisdiction.'
No case citations (X v. Y format) appear anywhere in the post.
No specific collateral-consequence claims appear; the post focuses on challenging breath test evidence rather than stating consequences of conviction.

results.reason: Frontmatter has no question_count field; body contains approximately 9 attorney-directed questions (calibration records, operator certification, bodycam review, etc.) with no frontmatter value to match against.

Three unsourced factual claims exceed the 2-claim threshold: calibration schedules (30/60/90 days), observation period duration (15-20 minutes), and RF interference susceptibility of older models — all stated as procedural/technical facts without inline sources.

Action items use plain, direct language ("Ask your attorney," "Write down," "Send this list") at or below 10th grade level, and technical terms like partition ratio are immediately explained in context.
Zero instances of the flagged cliche list found anywhere in the post.
Second person (you/your) maintained throughout; the single instance of "the defendant" appears inside a quoted prosecutor statement, not the narrator's voice.
Estimated 15-18% passive voice — constructions like "was last calibrated" and "is supposed to observe" appear but active voice dominates the majority of sentences.
Two legal terms used without definition on first use: "discovery requests" (Challenge Point 1 / What Attorney Should Request) and "suppression motions" (What Attorney Should Request section).
Logical flow from problem (BAC isn't a fact) → context (machine history) → four specific challenge points → action list → synthesis → CTA, with no orphaned paragraphs.
Multiple clear CTAs: numbered discovery request list to email to attorney, Case Progress Score link, DUI Defense Playbook link, and specific questions to ask at next meeting.
Action statements are direct and unhedged ("Ask your attorney," "Write down," "Send this list today"); hedging words like "could" appear only in informational/explanatory context about error margins.
No paragraph exceeds 300 words; action-oriented paragraphs ("Ask your attorney one question today," "Send your attorney this numbered list") stay well under 100 words.
Largest section (Challenge Point 3: Observation Period) is approximately 450 words out of ~3,000 total (~15%), well under the 50% threshold.

Every threat is paired with a specific action within 1-2 sentences — e.g., "scientifically compromised" → calibration checklist; "certification lapsed" → ask attorney to confirm; margin of error → five-minute conversation prompt.

Strong hook ("The number on the breathalyzer isn't a fact — it's an opinion from a machine"), evidence-rich middle with sourced claims and four structured challenge points, and empowering close with a concrete numbered action list.

results.evidence: Directives consistently target attorney communication ('Ask your attorney whether...', 'Send your attorney this numbered list') rather than independent legal action by the reader.

Every body section includes a proximate attorney redirect ('Ask your attorney one question today', 'Ask your attorney whether they've confirmed', etc.); FAQ answers reference 'your attorney' in FAQ 3.
Post uses conditional and general language ('could mean you were under the legal limit', 'yours may be one of them') rather than evaluating the reader's specific case strength.

Post recommends specific motions: 'your attorney should be using these gaps to file suppression motions' and 'that's a challenge your attorney needs to file — today, not next month' — naming the motion type and urging immediate filing.
No immigration consequences (deportation, visa status, DACA, green card) are discussed anywhere in the post.
No collateral consequences (professional license, housing, firearms, voting, student loans) are mentioned in the post.
Device names (Intoxilyzer 8000, Alco-Sensor FST, Draeger 9510) are breathalyzer models, not legal service providers; no law firms, bail bond companies, or public defenders are named.

'We' usage in 'What We Do' section describes the company's service ('We analyze DUI cases') rather than recommending legal actions; no 'we recommend', 'we advise', or 'we suggest' appears in legal-action context.

Multiple vivid second-person scenarios ('You're standing in a police station', 'The officer arrests you. You're in the back of the cruiser', 'Your attorney walks into your next meeting with a folder') are presented without hypothetical labels like 'Example scenario' or 'Imagine'.

Post consistently frames knowledge as empowering attorney communication: 'we find it and give you the questions to bring to your attorney', 'Ask your attorney this specific question', 'Five minutes of preparation unlocks months of defense'.

Legal rules are qualified throughout with 'typically every 30, 60, or 90 days depending on the model and jurisdiction', 'in most jurisdictions', 'varies by jurisdiction', and the disclaimer states 'Breathalyzer procedures and admissibility standards vary by state'.

'This is one of the strongest foundations for getting a DUI case dismissed' implies a specific outcome without qualifying that results vary by jurisdiction and circumstances; 'every gap is a weakness in their case' states case impact as certainty.

The four-point breathalyzer challenge framework (calibration, operator, observation, result) is presented as the blog's own legal strategy; 'The standard reference text on DUI defense' is cited without naming the specific text, author, or edition.
Legal statements are internally consistent throughout — error margins, calibration requirements, certification rules, and observation period requirements do not contradict each other.

Products are explicitly framed as preparation tools: 'identify exactly which records your attorney should be pulling', 'give you the questions to bring to your attorney'; disclaimer states 'We are not attorneys and do not provide legal representation'.

Opening hook is strong ('The number on the breathalyzer isn't a fact. It's an opinion from a machine.') but H2s 'The Machine Has a History' and 'The It's Just a Number Problem' are topical labels with no implied action for the reader.

Three legal terms used without inline definition on first use: 'BAC' (never expanded to Blood Alcohol Concentration), 'discovery requests' (used without explanation), and 'suppression motions' (linked but undefined). Hematocrit also undefined.

No concrete immediate-action block before the first H2. The TLDRBox contains a 'Your Next Step' but it requires contacting an attorney; the body intro (3 paragraphs) is pure reframing with no actionable step a reader can do alone right now.

Every section presents a single directive path — request calibration records, verify operator certification, challenge the observation period, question the margin of error. No section offers 3+ unranked options without a default recommendation.

'What Your Attorney Should Be Requesting' presents a 7-item numbered list with no priority grouping or 'start with these' marker — items 1-7 are all presented as equally important, exceeding the 5-item ungrouped threshold.
Single-post audit — pattern is system-decoder-post (decoding how breathalyzer machines work and mapping the four categories of challengeable evidence behind a BAC reading).

Every scary stat is paired with action within 2 sentences: '375+ DNA exonerations' paired with 'audit the process'; '.08 could be .06 to .10' paired with 'write down your BAC and the range'; overdue calibration paired with 'ask your attorney why they haven't challenged the reading.'

Zero blame language throughout — all accountability directed at the system ('departments miss calibration deadlines'), the machine ('the machine that produced it'), or the attorney ('if your attorney hasn't requested these records'). Reader is consistently positioned as the person being failed, not the person who failed.

Arc is strong — opening validates fear ('feels like a verdict'), middle converts unknown to known (four challenge points), and 'It's Just a Number' closes on agency ('Five minutes of preparation unlocks months of defense'). But the actual final H2 is the 'What We Do' CTA section, so the post's last words are a product pitch, not an agency statement.

No tables or H4+ headings, which is good. But key end-of-section actions ('Ask your attorney one question today', 'Look up your arrest date', 'Send your attorney this numbered list') are in regular paragraph text without bold formatting — buried where a phone reader scanning bold text would miss them.

Six of seven content H2 sections have strong bold screenshot sentences under 27 words (e.g., 'A breathalyzer overdue for calibration is a thermometer you haven't checked in months'). The 'What We Do' section has only CTA bold text, not a shareable insight a defendant would screenshot.

All 3 FAQ answers start with direct answers, run 2-4 sentences, and read like support-group replies ('The number on the screen is an estimate, not a fact' / 'If any category is missing or shows gaps, that is a weakness in the prosecution's case').
